summary:
Isaiah son of Amoz prophesied in Jerusalem "during the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah" (1:1) — the second half of the 700s BC, when Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel (722 BC) and invaded Judah itself (701). Isaiah and his contemporary Micah share a poem almost word for word — nations beating "their swords into plowshares" (2:4; Micah 4:1–3); who borrowed from whom is unknown. The book opens with an indictment — children reared by God have rebelled against Him (1:2); worship from hands "covered with blood" (1:15) is rejected — and an offer: "Though your sins are like scarlet, they will be as white as snow" (1:18).

Chapters 1–39 mostly address Isaiah's own Assyrian-era world. His call comes in chapter 6: in the year King Uzziah died he sees the Lord enthroned, seraphim ("burning ones" in Hebrew) crying "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts"; a coal from the altar cleanses his lips, and he answers, "Here am I. Send me!" To King Ahaz, shaken by two invading kings, he announces the sign of Immanuel, "God with us": "the virgin will be with child" (7:14). The Hebrew word almah can also mean simply "young woman"; Matthew 1:23 quotes the ancient Greek version's "virgin" at Jesus' birth. Later oracles (prophetic pronouncements) promise a royal child — "Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace" (9:6) — and a shoot "from the stump of Jesse" (11:1), David's father: new growth from a felled royal line. Oracles against the surrounding nations fill chapters 13–23; chapters 36–39 recount the Assyrian king Sennacherib's assault on Jerusalem in Hezekiah's reign, paralleling 2 Kings 18–20 almost word for word.

At chapter 40 the address shifts: "Comfort, comfort My people," says your God (40:1). These chapters speak to Judeans exiled in Babylon over a century after Isaiah's day and name their liberator: Cyrus, the Persian king who took Babylon in 539 BC and released the exiles (Ezra 1), called "My shepherd" (44:28) and "His anointed" (45:1) — Hebrew mashiach, the word behind "Messiah." Four poems, often called the Servant Songs (42:1–4; 49:1–6; 50:4–9; 52:13–53:12), describe a servant made "a light for the nations" (49:6) who suffers for others — "pierced for our transgressions" (53:5), "led like a lamb to the slaughter" (53:7). Who the servant is remains debated: Israel as a whole ("You are My Servant, Israel," 49:3), the prophet himself, or a coming individual. The New Testament applies chapter 53 to Jesus; in Acts 8:32–35 an Ethiopian official is reading it when Philip meets him.

Chapters 56–66 look past the return: foreigners and eunuchs welcomed into "a house of prayer for all the nations" (56:7), an anointed herald sent "to preach good news to the poor" (61:1), and "new heavens and a new earth" (65:17; repeated in 66:22), taken up in Revelation 21:1. Because chapters 40 onward presuppose the exile and name Cyrus, the book's composition is debated: the traditional view credits Isaiah of Jerusalem with all sixty-six chapters as long-range prophecy; many scholars assign chapters 40–66 to later writers in his tradition. On either view, the title "the Holy One of Israel" (1:4), rare elsewhere in the Old Testament, runs through every part of the book.

All four Gospels apply 40:3, "Prepare the way for the LORD," to John the Baptist (e.g. Mark 1:3); Jesus opens his ministry in Nazareth by reading 61:1–2 and declaring it fulfilled (Luke 4:17–21); Paul cites "a light for the nations" as his own commission (Acts 13:47); and "He will swallow up death forever" (25:8) supplies the climax of 1 Corinthians 15:54. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls is a complete Isaiah copied around the second century BC — the Great Isaiah Scroll, roughly a thousand years older than the oldest complete Hebrew manuscripts previously known. The book ends with all mankind coming "to worship before Me" (66:23) and, in its final verse, the corpses of the rebels whose "worm will never die" (66:24) — the line Jesus quotes in his warning about hell (Mark 9:48).
